explanations.explanation: Yes, Saul. Verse 1 says the LORD delivered David “…from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” The song names Saul right alongside all the rest. Saul was Israel's king, the one Samuel was sent to anoint (1 Samuel 15:1). Good eye, baker.

Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath (1 Samuel 17:4), has a story so famous it crashes every David party. But this verse doesn't name him. It says the LORD delivered David “…from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” The name at the end is Saul.

Absalom, David's son (2 Samuel 3:3), is a name that's easy to reach for, but he never gets invited to this verse. Verse 1 ends with “…and from the hand of Saul.” That's the name David's song sets apart. Saul it is.

Rock, fortress, stronghold, refuge. David even says “…in whom I take refuge…” in verse 3. These are all spots you run to when trouble's chasing you. Picture a hole in a cliff, and you've got the idea.

I see why you'd go there, since David is singing to the LORD. But a rock and a fortress aren't worship spots in this song. David calls God “…my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield…” These pictures are about being kept safe.

Nobody's haggling over prices at a fortress, friend. David uses “refuge” and “shield” right alongside these words, and those are about protection. These pictures are all about staying safe, not shopping.

David says, “I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies.” That's David speaking about himself. He says he will call, and he says he will be saved. Saved is the word.
Hiding is a fair guess after all those fortress words. But verse 4 uses a different word. David says, “so shall I be saved from my enemies.” Saved is the word.
Running isn't in verse 4. David says, “so shall I be saved from my enemies.” The word is saved. Running is what I do when the timer goes off and the batch is burning.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Verse 7 says, “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God.” David is entangled in the cords of Sheol, and the song says he cries out to God. That's a good thing to remember on a tangled-up day.

Fighting loose sounds like a king, I'll give you that. But verse 7 says, “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God.” The song has David crying out to God. Fighting his way loose isn't what the verse says.
Calling the soldiers makes sense for a king. But look at verse 7: “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God.” Soldiers don't show up in this part of the song. His cry goes to God.
Verse 7 says the opposite: “…from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears.” His cry made it all the way. So this one is false.
Right, it's false. David says, “And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears.” The cry reached God. Nothing got lost in the mail.
Verse 8 says the earth shook and quaked, “they were shaken because He burned with anger.” David gives the reason in the same verse. The shaking comes from the LORD Himself.
An army marching would shake the ground, sure. But verse 8 gives a different reason: “they were shaken because He burned with anger.” No army is named in that verse. The LORD's anger is the cause.
The sea shows up later in the song, in verse 16, but not as the reason here. Verse 8 says, “they were shaken because He burned with anger.” That's the answer David gives.
Verse 11 says, “He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind.” That's David's picture of the LORD coming to rescue him. You nailed it.
It's true, so this one's a miss. Verse 11 says, “He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind.” Those words are right there in the song.

Verse 15 says the opposite: “He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them.” Nobody is holding their ground there. The foes are scattered and routed. So this one is false.
Right, false. The foes don't hold anything. Verse 15 says, “He shot His arrows and scattered the foes…” They're scattered and routed.

explanations.answer: He reaches down and draws him out
explanations.explanation: Verse 17 says, “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters.” David was in the waves of death, and the LORD took hold of him personally. That's a mighty close rescue.

explanations.answer: He calms the waves all around him
explanations.explanation: Calming waves makes sense, but verse 17 describes something closer. It says, “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters.” The LORD takes hold of David and draws him out.

explanations.answer: He sends an angel to lift him up
explanations.explanation: An angel would be a nice touch, but this verse doesn't mention one. It says, “He reached down from on high and took hold of me…” The LORD Himself does the reaching.
David says, “He rescued me because He delighted in me.” That's the reason right in verse 20. Being delighted in is a sweet thing to hear.
David did cry out in verse 7, but he doesn't call that the reason for the rescue. Verse 20 says, “He rescued me because He delighted in me.” The reason is God's delight.
No insults are mentioned in this part of the song. The reason David gives is in verse 20: “He rescued me because He delighted in me.” The LORD's delight is the reason.

explanations.answer: He kept the ways of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David says in verse 22, “For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.” That's what he points to. It's about staying on the LORD's path.

explanations.answer: He won every battle he fought
explanations.explanation: Battles come up later in the song, but verse 22 points somewhere else. David says, “For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.” He's pointing to keeping the LORD's ways.

explanations.answer: He built the LORD a temple
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son, was the one who built the temple (1 Kings 8:20). In this song, David points to something else in verse 22: “For I have kept the ways of the LORD…” That's his answer.
David says the reverse in verse 23: “I have not disregarded His statutes.” He says the LORD's ordinances are before him. Setting them aside is not what he claims.

Right, it's false. In verse 23, David says, “For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes.” He's keeping them in front of him. Setting them aside is the opposite of what he sings.
Verse 26 says, “To the faithful You show Yourself faithful…” David sings it to God, and the verse says “You.” So the statement is true just as written. Well done.
It's true, so this one is a miss. Verse 26 says, “To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless…” David says it right to God.
It sounds like it'd match the pattern, but verse 27 breaks it. David says, “…to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.” The word is shrewd, not crooked.

Right, it's false. Verse 27 says, “…but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.” The word at the end is shrewd, not crooked. The lines before it match up word for word, but this one changes at that spot.
Verse 28 says, “You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.” The afflicted get saved, and the haughty get brought down. David puts both in one breath.
Rewarding strength sounds nice, but verse 28 says the opposite. It reads, “…Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.” Bringing down is the purpose.
The verse doesn't say anything about extra time. It says, “…Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.” The haughty are brought down.

explanations.answer: Charge an army and scale a wall
explanations.explanation: David sings, “For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.” Charging an army and climbing a wall both look like jobs for a crowd, and he says he can do them in God. I'd need a ladder, a pep talk and a nap.

explanations.answer: Rule the land without any help
explanations.explanation: Without any help is the opposite of this verse. David says, “…in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.” The “in You” and “with my God…” are the whole point.
Egypt's chariots don't show up in this verse. Verse 30 says, “For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.” An army and a wall are what he names.
Verse 32 asks, “For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?” Those are questions with an obvious answer, and David's answer is nobody. The LORD stands alone in the song.
David is asking, “For who is God besides the LORD?” and he isn't leaving room for a list. The next question, “…who is the Rock except our God?”, points the same way. No one else is named.
Verse 32 asks the questions with no priest in sight. David asks, “For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?” He's not waiting on a vote.
David says, “He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze.” It's the LORD who does the training. Your hands, my mustache, same idea.
Building is a good use for hands, but verse 35 says something else. It reads, “He trains my hands for battle…” Building isn't in the verse.
David did tend sheep (1 Samuel 16:11), but that's not what this verse says. Verse 35 reads, “He trains my hands for battle…” Shepherding isn't in the verse. The answer is battle.
Verse 35 says, “my arms can bend a bow of bronze.” David sings it right after saying the LORD trains his hands for battle. So the statement is true. Good job.
It's true, so this one's a miss. David says, “my arms can bend a bow of bronze.” in verse 35. I couldn't bend a pipe cleaner.
David says to the LORD, “…Your gentleness exalts me.” Right in the middle of all that battle talk, a soft word like gentleness shows up. It's the kind of detail you'd miss if you were rushing.
David does talk about strength in this song, but he gives God the credit. Verse 36 says, “…Your gentleness exalts me.” It's God's gentleness that lifts him.
His army's courage isn't mentioned in this verse. David says to the LORD, “…Your gentleness exalts me.” That's the thing that lifts him.
The second half is where this goes off. Verse 37 says, “You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way.” His ankles hold.

Right, it's false. Verse 37 says, “You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way.” The path gets wider, and his ankles do not give way. The second half of the statement is where it goes off. Nice work.
David says to the LORD, “You have armed me with strength for battle…” The strength comes from God. David sings it as a gift.

Wisdom would be handy in battle, and I could use a double batch of it myself. But verse 40 says, “You have armed me with strength for battle…” Wisdom isn't the word. David names strength, and he sings it to the LORD.

Armor, huh? I'd show up to a battle in an apron and a chef's hat, so I'm no expert. Verse 40 says, “You have armed me with strength for battle…” The gift David names is strength, not armor. And he sings it to the LORD.
Verse 42 says the opposite: “They looked, but there was no one to save them—to the LORD, but He did not answer.” They looked to the LORD, and He did not answer them. So this one is false.

Right, it's false. Verse 42 says, “They looked, but there was no one to save them—to the LORD, but He did not answer.” The enemies look to the LORD, and no answer comes. That makes the statement false. Well done.
David says to the LORD, “You have delivered me from the strife of my people…” This verse names his own people. Strife is the word that fills the blank.
Hunger would be a rough thing to face, but verse 44 doesn't say it. It says, “You have delivered me from the strife of my people…” Strife is the word.
Sickness isn't in this verse. David says, “You have delivered me from the strife of my people…” The right word is strife.
Verse 45 says, “Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me.” Cowering and obeying, both in one verse. David sings it as part of what the LORD has done for him.
Mocking doesn't show up here. Verse 45 says, “Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me.” They cower and obey.

explanations.answer: They march out to fight him
explanations.explanation: Verse 45 says, “Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me.” Cowering is what the verse gives, not marching out to fight. The word for them is cower.
Verse 48 says the LORD is “…the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me…” Nations are brought down beneath David, not lifted above him. So this one is false.
Right, it's false. Verse 48 praises “…the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me…” The nations go beneath David, not above him. So the statement has it backward. Well done.

explanations.answer: Praise the LORD and sing to His name
explanations.explanation: David says, “Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name.” After the rescue comes the praise. This song is part of it.

explanations.answer: Build altars to the LORD in every land
explanations.explanation: Altars would be a big project, but verse 50 doesn't say them. David says, “Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name.” He'll praise and sing.

explanations.answer: Send gifts to the LORD from every land
explanations.explanation: Gifts sound generous, but verse 50 doesn't mention them. David says, “…I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name.” Praise and singing are the plan.
David closes with, “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” It's not only David, and it's not only his lifetime. The song ends on forever.
That's too small for the closing line. David says, “…to David and his descendants forever.” His descendants are in it, and so is forever.

explanations.answer: The soldiers who fought beside him
explanations.explanation: Soldiers don't show up in the last verse. David says the LORD shows loving devotion “…to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” That's who is named.
Verse 51 says, “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” David is the anointed one the song names. That's right there in the song's closing words. Sharp work.
It's true, so this one is a miss. Verse 51 says, “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” David is called His anointed.
